ગુરુ. Those we learned from

Thirty-four teachers

Nobody on this coast invented the lever, the honest ledger or the question asked before the work begins. We borrowed them. A firm should say whom it borrowed from.

NKovaya

There are thirty-four names here. Eleven wrote. Ten measured the world. Eight painted, carved or argued. Five led. None of them built a cement plant. Each of them knew something that a person who builds one needs to know.

For each teacher we give one thing that really happened, told plainly, and then what we took from it. We have put no words in anyone’s mouth.

Eleven who wrote

Shakespeare, Meghani, Premchand, Tagore, Homer, Dante, Kalidasa, Tolstoy, Ghalib, Austen, Dostoevsky.

Ten who measured

Archimedes, Einstein, Newton, Ramanujan, Tesla, Curie, Galileo, Aryabhata, Kalam, Darwin.

Eight who saw

Leonardo, Michelangelo, Socrates, Chanakya, Plato, Van Gogh, Ravi Varma, Picasso.

Five who led

Alexander, Shivaji Maharaj, Ashoka, Genghis Khan, Vasco da Gama.

Three to begin with

One who walked this very country with a notebook. One whose law is printed on the card inside every crane. One whose word is still cut in a rock a hundred and twenty kilometres from our gate.

Jhaverchand Meghani

Gujarati folk literature, 1896 to 1947

He walked Kathiawar from village to village with a notebook and wrote down what the bards and the grandmothers remembered, before it could be lost. The result was the five volumes of Saurashtra ni Rasdhar. Gandhi called him the national poet. Most of his heroes were not kings. They were ordinary people who had given their word and would not take it back.

What we tookA firm is the promises it kept on the days when keeping them was expensive. We write ours down with their dates, and we call them kathas.

Where it lives on this site: Our story

Jhaverchand Meghani on an Indian postage stamp of 1999.

Archimedes

Mathematics and mechanics, About 287 to 212 BCE

He proved the law of the lever: weights balance at distances inversely proportional to their size. Tradition adds a boast, that given a place to stand he could move the earth, a screw that lifts water, and a great claw that hoisted Roman ships out of the harbour at Syracuse.

What we tookA crane’s load chart is his law printed on a card. Push the load farther out and the crane can lift less. Our riggers read the card before anyone touches the hook.

Where it lives on this site: Mobile cranes

Archimedes as Domenico Fetti imagined him in 1620.

Ashoka

Kingship, Reigned about 268 to 232 BCE

About a hundred and twenty kilometres from Kovaya, at the foot of Girnar, his edicts are cut into a great boulder in the speech of ordinary people. The second of them records wells dug and trees planted along the roads for the use of people and animals, and medicine provided for both.

What we tookShade, water and care for whoever is on the road: it is the oldest welfare order in Gujarat. At our work fronts it takes the form of a clay pot of cool water and a rule about the afternoon sun.

Where it lives on this site: Heat and monsoon

Ashoka's edicts cut into the rock at Girnar.

All thirty-four, and where each one lives on this site

Every teacher is tied to one page of our own work. Follow the name to the story, or the page to the work.

Literature, writing and poetry

Eleven who wrote

A writer’s trade is to say a true thing so that it cannot be misunderstood. That is also the trade of whoever writes a safety rule, a work order or a promise.

6 min read

NKovaya
On this page
  1. Why writers
Thirty-four teachers
  • Thirty-four teachers overview

The teachers

  • Eleven who wrote
  • Ten who measured
  • Eight who saw
  • Five who led

Why writers

Most of what goes wrong between a client and a contractor goes wrong in words. A scope that could be read two ways. A rule nobody could follow because nobody could read it. A promise that was never quite made.

These eleven spent their lives making words do exactly what was meant.

Jhaverchand Meghani

Gujarati folk literature, 1896 to 1947

He walked Kathiawar from village to village with a notebook and wrote down what the bards and the grandmothers remembered, before it could be lost. The result was the five volumes of Saurashtra ni Rasdhar. Gandhi called him the national poet. Most of his heroes were not kings. They were ordinary people who had given their word and would not take it back.

What we tookA firm is the promises it kept on the days when keeping them was expensive. We write ours down with their dates, and we call them kathas.

Where it lives on this site: Our story

Jhaverchand Meghani on an Indian postage stamp of 1999.

William Shakespeare

Playwriting and poetry, 1564 to 1616

In the last days of December 1598 his company had a problem that every contractor will recognise: a lease that had run out and a landlord who wanted the building. So they took their own playhouse apart, carried its oak frame across London, and raised it again south of the river as the Globe. The greatest plays in the language opened inside a structure that had been dismantled, moved and re-erected by the people who used it.

What we tookSteel can be taken down as carefully as it went up, and be right the second time. We number every piece before a bolt is loosened.

Where it lives on this site: Structural steel erection

The Chandos portrait, thought to be of Shakespeare, painted about 1600 to 1610.

Munshi Premchand

Hindi and Urdu realist fiction, 1880 to 1936

In his story Namak ka Daroga a young salt inspector stops a rich man’s carts at night and is offered more money than he will earn in a lifetime to look the other way. He refuses, and it costs him his post. The story does not pretend that honesty is cheap. It shows what it is worth, because in the end the rich man comes looking for the one person he could not buy.

What we tookJafrabad still makes salt, and the offer has not changed in a hundred years. Nobody working under our name gives or takes a rupee for a favour.

Where it lives on this site: Anti-bribery and gifts

Munshi Premchand.

Rabindranath Tagore

Bengali literature and poetry, 1861 to 1941

At seventeen he lived for some months in an old palace beside the Sabarmati at Shahibaug in Ahmedabad, and its empty rooms later became his story The Hungry Stones. Years afterwards, in Gitanjali, he asked for a country where the mind is without fear and the head is held high.

What we tookA site where people are afraid to speak is a site waiting for an accident. Our speak-up line exists so that the newest helper can report a wrong without fear.

Where it lives on this site: Speak up

Rabindranath Tagore in 1909.

Homer

Epic poetry, About the eighth century BCE

Before the fighting starts, the Iliad stops to count. Its second book lists the Greek fleet contingent by contingent: who came, from where, under which captain, with how many ships. Scholars add it up to 1,186. Audiences sat through it gladly, because a muster roll honestly called is a kind of poetry.

What we tookOur machinery pages are a catalogue of ships. Every class, every tonnage, what it is for and what it will not do.

Where it lives on this site: Heavy machinery

Homer as the ancient world imagined him. A Roman marble bust in the British Museum.

Dante Alighieri

Medieval poetry, 1265 to 1321

He could have written in Latin for scholars. He wrote in the Italian of the street, so that a wool merchant could read about heaven and hell. And when he wanted a picture of hard work he described the shipyard of Venice in winter: men boiling pitch, caulking seams, shaping oars and patching sails.

What we tookA rule that a worker cannot read protects nobody. Ours are in Gujarati, Hindi and English, in the fewest words we can manage.

Where it lives on this site: Life-saving rules

Dante, painted by Sandro Botticelli about 1495.

Kalidasa

Classical Sanskrit poetry and drama, About the fourth or fifth century CE

The Ritusamhara, the poem of the seasons that tradition gives to him, walks through the six seasons of the Indian year one at a time, beginning with summer: the pools shrinking, the wind hot, and then the rains arriving like a king, with cloud for elephants and thunder for drums.

What we tookThis coast still works to six seasons and not four. Our calendar plans the year the way he wrote it: by heat, by cloud, and by the clear weather after.

Where it lives on this site: The calendar of the coast

Shakuntala, the heroine of Kalidasa's best-known play, painted by Raja Ravi Varma.

Leo Tolstoy

The novel, 1828 to 1910

In How Much Land Does a Man Need? a peasant is promised all the land he can walk around between sunrise and sunset. He walks too far, runs back as the light goes, and falls dead at the finish. His servant buries him in six feet of ground, which turns out to be all he needed.

What we tookA shutdown is the same bargain: a fixed sunset, and a list of work that always wants to grow. Our playbook freezes the list before the first day, so that the plant lights up on time.

Where it lives on this site: The shutdown playbook

Leo Tolstoy in 1908, in a colour photograph by Sergei Prokudin-Gorsky.

Mirza Ghalib

Urdu and Persian poetry, 1797 to 1869

The greatest Urdu poet of his century spent years of his life chasing money that was owed to him. He travelled from Delhi to Calcutta to petition for his family’s pension, waited the better part of two years, and came home with poems and debts.

What we tookNobody should have to chase what they have earned. Our partners are paid on the day we said, and the page on payments tells them who to call if they are not.

Where it lives on this site: Payments

Mirza Ghalib, in a photograph taken in the 1860s.

Jane Austen

English fiction, 1775 to 1817

In a letter of 1816 she described her own work as a little bit of ivory, two inches wide, on which she worked with so fine a brush that it showed little effect for much labour. Six novels came off that ivory, and not a careless sentence in any of them.

What we tookA mill is aligned on shims thinner than a visiting card. There the fineness is the whole job.

Where it lives on this site: Alignment and grouting

Jane Austen, sketched by her sister Cassandra about 1810.

Fyodor Dostoevsky

Literature and human psychology, 1821 to 1881

Before he was a novelist he was an engineer. He trained at the military engineering school in St Petersburg and worked as a draughtsman. Then came four years in a Siberian labour camp, and the book he made of it, in which the convicts are, before anything else, men.

What we tookA code of conduct is conscience written down by people who know the work. Ours begins with how we treat the person at the bottom of the scaffold.

Where it lives on this site: Code of conduct

Fyodor Dostoevsky, painted by Vasily Perov in 1872.

Science, mathematics and engineering

Ten who measured

Every one of these ten refused to take somebody’s word for it. They weighed, counted, timed and tested. On a site that habit has a name. It is called inspection.

5 min read

NKovaya
On this page
  1. Why those who measured
Thirty-four teachers
  • Thirty-four teachers overview

The teachers

  • Eleven who wrote
  • Ten who measured
  • Eight who saw
  • Five who led

Why those who measured

A load chart, a cube test, a torque value, a tide table. Our working day is full of numbers that somebody once had the patience to find out.

Archimedes

Mathematics and mechanics, About 287 to 212 BCE

He proved the law of the lever: weights balance at distances inversely proportional to their size. Tradition adds a boast, that given a place to stand he could move the earth, a screw that lifts water, and a great claw that hoisted Roman ships out of the harbour at Syracuse.

What we tookA crane’s load chart is his law printed on a card. Push the load farther out and the crane can lift less. Our riggers read the card before anyone touches the hook.

Where it lives on this site: Mobile cranes

Archimedes as Domenico Fetti imagined him in 1620.

Albert Einstein

Theoretical physics, 1879 to 1955

In 1905 he was a patent examiner in Bern, checking other people’s inventions. In his own hours that year he published four papers that rebuilt physics. One of them showed that time is not the same for everyone. It depends on where you stand and how you are moving.

What we tookOn a stopped kiln, time also depends on where you stand. A crew twenty-five minutes away and a crew five hours away are not living in the same emergency.

Where it lives on this site: Proximity

Albert Einstein in 1921, photographed by Ferdinand Schmutzer.

Isaac Newton

Physics and mathematics, 1642 to 1727

The man who explained gravity spent his last thirty years at the Royal Mint. As its Warden he went after counterfeiters in person, took statements in taverns and prisons, and saw the most notorious of them, William Chaloner, convicted in 1699.

What we tookFalse coin today is a forged work order, or a job sold for a fee. Our fraud alert says what a genuine ATKAYVA message looks like, and what we never ask for.

Where it lives on this site: Fraud alert

Isaac Newton in 1689, painted by Godfrey Kneller.

Srinivasa Ramanujan

Pure mathematics, 1887 to 1920

In 1912 he took a clerk’s post in the accounts section of the Madras Port Trust at thirty rupees a month. He kept the port’s books by day and did mathematics that Cambridge would soon struggle to follow. The first people to back him were the port’s own officers.

What we tookSomeone at a port desk is always worth more than the desk suggests. And a ledger kept by a careful clerk is the reason a cargo bill can be trusted.

Where it lives on this site: Port cargo

Srinivasa Ramanujan.

Nikola Tesla

Electrical engineering, 1856 to 1943

His induction motor of 1888 has no brushes and nothing that sparks. A rotating magnetic field drags the rotor round after it. Together with alternating current it meant that power could be made at Niagara and used in a factory miles away.

What we tookEvery mill drive and fan in a cement works is his motor, grown large. We set them on their foundations, and we are getting ready for the wind and sun that will feed them.

Where it lives on this site: Energy

Nikola Tesla about 1890.

Marie Curie

Radioactivity and chemistry, 1867 to 1934

In the First World War she fitted X-ray sets into motor cars and drove them to the front herself, so that surgeons could see the shrapnel before they cut. The soldiers called the cars little Curies. She trained the operators as well.

What we tookA test is only useful where the work is. Cubes are cast at the pour, welds are checked at the joint, and the laboratory’s report goes into the handover file.

Where it lives on this site: Quality

Marie Curie about 1920.

Galileo Galilei

Astronomy and the science of materials, 1564 to 1642

His last book, Two New Sciences, opens in the shipyard of Venice with a builder’s puzzle: why does a large structure fail when a small one of the same shape stands? His answer, that weight grows faster than strength as things get bigger, is where structural engineering begins.

What we tookIt is why a big foundation is not a small footing made larger. Large pours, heavy blocks and long spans each get their own arithmetic.

Where it lives on this site: Civil and structural works

Galileo Galilei, painted by Justus Sustermans.

Aryabhata

Mathematics and astronomy, 476 to about 550 CE

At twenty-three he wrote the Aryabhatiya: a table of sines, a value of pi good to four places, and the plain statement that the stars appear to move because the earth turns. His arithmetic runs on the Indian place-value system, the one that gave the world its zero.

What we tookWe keep three zeros of our own: zero harm, zero reportable lost-time incidents so far, and zero interference with the client. Our numbers page says exactly how each is counted.

Where it lives on this site: Numbers, and how we count them

A modern statue of Aryabhata at Pune. No likeness of him survives.

A. P. J. Abdul Kalam

Aerospace engineering, 1931 to 2015

He grew up on the island of Rameswaram, the son of a boat owner. In 1979 the rocket he was responsible for fell into the sea. His chairman, Satish Dhawan, faced the press and took the blame himself. A year later the next launch succeeded, and Dhawan sent Kalam out to take the applause.

What we tookWhen a job goes wrong, the leadership answers for it. When it goes right, the crew is named. We mean to grow on those terms.

Where it lives on this site: The road ahead

A. P. J. Abdul Kalam in 2008.

Charles Darwin

Evolutionary biology, 1809 to 1882

His last book was not about finches. It was about earthworms. He weighed their castings for years and reckoned that on good English land they bring more than ten tons of earth to the surface of every acre, every year. The quiet repetition of small loads, he showed, reshapes a country.

What we tookAn excavator is a very large worm with a fuel tank. Bucket by bucket is still how a foundation pit, a quarry and a breakwater are made.

Where it lives on this site: Excavators

Charles Darwin in the 1850s.

1. Home

  3. Eight who saw

Arts, philosophy and statecraft

Eight who saw

A painter, a sculptor and a philosopher have this in common with a good site engineer. They look at the thing itself, for a long time, before they touch it.

4 min read

NKovaya
On this page
  1. Why those who saw
Thirty-four teachers
  • Thirty-four teachers overview

The teachers

  • Eleven who wrote
  • Ten who measured
  • Eight who saw
  • Five who led

Why those who saw

Half of engineering is seeing what is actually in front of you and not what the drawing says should be there. The other half is asking the question nobody wants asked.

Leonardo da Vinci

Art and invention, 1452 to 1519

About 1482 he wrote to the Duke of Milan asking for work. The letter lists what he could do: light bridges, ways to drain a moat, siege machines, tunnels, ships, buildings, canals. Only in the last lines does he add that he can also paint as well as any man.

What we tookIt is the oldest capability statement we know of. Ours follows his order: say plainly what you can build, and let the art come as a surprise.

Where it lives on this site: Capabilities

A drawing in red chalk of about 1512, generally taken to be Leonardo's portrait of himself.

Michelangelo

Sculpture and architecture, 1475 to 1564

For the better part of three years, at the height of his powers, he carved almost nothing. The Pope had sent him into the mountains above Pietrasanta to open new marble quarries, and he spent the time building a road to bring the blocks down to the sea. He held that the figure is already inside the stone, and that the sculptor only removes what hides it.

What we tookRock excavation is the same act at a larger scale. Remove exactly what is not the foundation, and stop.

Where it lives on this site: Rock excavation

Michelangelo about 1545, in a portrait attributed to Daniele da Volterra.

Socrates

Philosophy, About 470 to 399 BCE

He wrote nothing down. He stood in the marketplace of Athens and asked questions until the person answering found out what he did not know. He claimed only one piece of wisdom for himself: that he knew how little he knew.

What we tookOur toolbox talk is his method in ten minutes. What are we doing today? What can hurt us? What have we done about it? Who is new?

Where it lives on this site: Safety

Socrates. A Roman marble head in the Louvre.

Chanakya (Kautilya)

Statecraft, About the fourth century BCE

The Arthashastra is a manual for running a state, down to mines, wages and the audit of stores. It is unsentimental about money. An official who handles revenue, it says, is like a man with honey on his tongue, and catching him is like telling whether a fish is drinking the water it swims in. So it prescribes ledgers, inspectors and the rotation of posts.

What we tookWe assume the honey is always on the tongue. Vigilance is not suspicion of people. It is a system that does not need them to be saints.

Where it lives on this site: Vigilance

The Arthashastra on palm leaves. This copy came to light at Mysore in 1905.

Plato

Philosophy, About 428 to 348 BCE

Tradition says the door of his Academy carried a warning: let no one ignorant of geometry enter. In the Republic he tells of prisoners in a cave who take the shadows on the wall for the real thing, until one of them walks out into the sun.

What we tookA drawing is geometry, and a daily report is a shadow. Our engineers check the first before we build, and walk the site to see the second for themselves.

Where it lives on this site: Engineering review

Plato. A Roman marble copy of a Greek portrait, in the Capitoline Museums.

Vincent van Gogh

Painting, 1853 to 1890

In his last winter, at Saint-Rémy, he painted the road menders: workmen relaying a street under the great plane trees, with their heaps of sand and stone in the foreground. He painted sowers, diggers and weavers with the same attention he gave a starry night, and sold almost nothing.

What we tookSomebody thought road work deserved a master’s canvas. We try to build roads that deserve it.

Where it lives on this site: Roads and drainage

Vincent van Gogh, a self-portrait of September 1889.

Raja Ravi Varma

Painting, 1848 to 1906

He painted for the courts of Travancore and Baroda, the state to which Amreli then belonged. In 1894 he did something no court painter had done. He set up a lithographic press and printed his pictures by the thousand, so that a farmer could hang on his wall the same image as a maharaja.

What we tookGood work that cannot be repeated is only a performance. In 2019 we wrote our method down, so that the tenth job is done like the best one.

Where it lives on this site: How a job runs

Raja Ravi Varma on an Indian postage stamp of 1971.

Pablo Picasso

Modern art, 1881 to 1973

Over six weeks in the winter of 1945 he drew a bull on a lithographic stone eleven times. The first is all muscle and hide. Each state after it has less, until the last is a few lines, and still nothing but a bull.

What we tookZero interference is the same exercise. Take the phone calls, the vendors and the paperwork out of the client’s day until only the finished job is left.

Where it lives on this site: The whole job, one order

Pablo Picasso in 1962.

Exploration, strategy and leadership

Five who led

A causeway built into the sea. A relay of fresh horses. A navy raised from nothing. A pilot who knew the monsoon. An edict in the people’s own speech. These are five answers to one question: how do you get many people to do a hard thing well?

4 min read

NKovaya
On this page
  1. Why those who led
  2. The dam that was repaired three times
  3. The pilot from Gujarat
Thirty-four teachers
  • Thirty-four teachers overview

The teachers

  • Eleven who wrote
  • Ten who measured
  • Eight who saw
  • Five who led

Why those who led

An emergency call-out and a twelve-day shutdown are both small campaigns. Somebody has to decide, somebody has to be obeyed, and everybody has to come home.

Ashoka

Kingship, Reigned about 268 to 232 BCE

About a hundred and twenty kilometres from Kovaya, at the foot of Girnar, his edicts are cut into a great boulder in the speech of ordinary people. The second of them records wells dug and trees planted along the roads for the use of people and animals, and medicine provided for both.

What we tookShade, water and care for whoever is on the road: it is the oldest welfare order in Gujarat. At our work fronts it takes the form of a clay pot of cool water and a rule about the afternoon sun.

Where it lives on this site: Heat and monsoon

Ashoka's edicts cut into the rock at Girnar.

The rock at the foot of Girnar, about a hundred and twenty kilometres from Kovaya. Ashoka’s edicts are cut into it, and so is a later record of the repair of a dam.

The dam that was repaired three times

The same rock carries a second story, and it is a contractor’s story.

It records a reservoir called Sudarshana, built near Girnar in the time of Chandragupta Maurya by his governor Pushyagupta. Under Ashoka another governor, Tushaspha, added canals to it. About the year 150 a great storm burst the dam. The ruler Rudradaman had it rebuilt stronger than before, and had the fact cut into the rock. Three centuries later it failed again, and was repaired again.

So the oldest maintenance record in Gujarat is on that boulder. A structure was built, damaged by weather, and put right, and somebody thought the repair worth writing down. We agree with them. See Maintenance and shutdowns.

Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj

Leadership and strategy, 1630 to 1680

He built a navy where none had been thought necessary, and raised sea forts such as Sindhudurg on rock off the Konkan coast. He moved faster than larger armies because he knew the ground. And his orders to his own soldiers were strict: take nothing from the cultivator, not even a stalk of grass, without paying for it.

What we tookWe work as guests in other people’s plants and villages. Speed and knowledge of the ground are our trade. Leaving nothing damaged behind us is our rule.

Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj, in a portrait of the 1680s now in the British Museum.

Alexander the Great

Strategy, 356 to 323 BCE

Tyre stood on an island half a mile off the coast and had never been taken. In 332 BCE he had his army build a causeway of stone and timber out through the sea to its walls. It took seven months. Sand has gathered against that causeway ever since, and Tyre is no longer an island.

What we tookA jetty is a decision to walk into the sea and keep going. This coast has several, and each began as one tipper of rock.

Where it lives on this site: Ports and logistics

Alexander, from the mosaic of his battle with Darius found at Pompeii.

Genghis Khan

Organisation and speed, About 1162 to 1227

The empire he founded ran on a relay. Post stations a day’s ride apart kept fresh horses ready, and a rider with the right token could cover in a day what an army covered in a week. His soldiers were organised in tens, hundreds and thousands, and each unit answered to one named leader.

What we tookAn emergency crew is a relay too: someone always saddled, a gang of ten with one leader, and a number that is answered at night.

Where it lives on this site: Emergency response

Genghis Khan, in a portrait painted for the Yuan court decades after his death.

Vasco da Gama

Navigation, About 1460 to 1524

He reached Calicut in May 1498 and opened the sea road from Europe. But his ships did not find India by themselves. At Malindi on the African coast he took aboard a pilot who knew the monsoon, a man the Portuguese chroniclers describe as a Gujarati, and that pilot brought the fleet across in little more than three weeks.

What we tookThe famous captain needed someone who knew this water. Local knowledge is not a courtesy. It is the route.

Where it lives on this site: Transport and heavy haulage

A portrait of about 1525 to 1550, long said to be of Vasco da Gama.

The pilot from Gujarat

Long before Vasco da Gama needed a pilot who knew this sea, people on this coast had been building for it. The basin at Lothal is some four thousand years old. Whatever else is argued about it, it is brick laid to hold water by people who understood the tide.

Local knowledge is not a courtesy. It is the route. See Proximity.
